title: "Downloads are cheap"
subtitle: "Validated use as a measure of research software"
author:
  # TODO before submission: affiliation and ORCID. Left blank deliberately
  # and not filled in with a plausible guess.
  - name: Gaurav Sood
    email: gsood07@gmail.com
    affiliation: ""
    orcid: ""
date: today
keywords:
  - research software
  - software citation
  - replication
  - metascience
  - Stata
  - static analysis
abstract: |
  Counts of research software use allocate credit, and the available ones are cheap to produce: a download is one fetch of a file. I propose validated use, a package loaded in replication code deposited at a journal that checks it, as a costly signal, and measure it in `{python} f"{n_deposits_analyzable:,}"` deposits from `{python} f"{n_collections_tallied:,}"` economics and political science journal collections, which load `{python} f"{len(usage):,}"` R, Python and Stata packages. Among packages the corpus uses, validated use and downloads agree loosely, and least where automatic installation is commonest: the rank correlation is `{python} f"{agree['ssc']['used']['rho']:.2f}"` for Stata, `{python} f"{agree['cran']['used']['rho']:.2f}"` for R and `{python} f"{agree['pypi']['used']['rho']:.2f}"` for Python. Downloads track a package's position in the dependency graph more closely than its use. The most used software prepares exhibits: `{python} top_stata_package` is in `{python} f"{top_stata_share:.0%}"` of Stata deposits. Stata appears in `{python} f"{stata_to_r_ratio:.1f}"` times as many deposits as R and is missing from studies of research software because its packages are scattered across SSC, two journals' archives and authors' sites with no index across them. I build that index, `{python} f"{n_index_commands:,}"` commands in `{python} f"{n_index_packages:,}"` packages, and release it with the mention-level data.
bibliography: references.bib
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    code-fold: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
---

```{python}
#| label: setup
# Every number in this paper is computed here and inserted by reference. None is
# typed into the prose. That makes "regenerate the paper" and "check the paper"
# the same operation, which is the only version of reproducibility that survives
# a revision.
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import duckdb
import pandas as pd

from softverse.build.downloads import agreement
from softverse.build.downloads import read as read_versus
from softverse.model.enums import NON_USE_CONSTRUCTS
from softverse.registries.load import INDEX_FILE
from softverse.registries.lock import pinned_directory, read_lock
from softverse.stata.builtins import curated
from softverse.stata.index import credited

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).parent if "__file__" in dir() else "."))
from exhibits import figure, table  # noqa: E402

TALLY = Path("../build/tally")
con = duckdb.connect()
mentions = con.execute(f"SELECT * FROM '{TALLY}/mentions.parquet'").df()
files = con.execute(f"SELECT * FROM '{TALLY}/files.parquet'").df()
usage = pd.read_csv(TALLY / "usage_by_package.csv")
presence = pd.read_csv(TALLY / "language_presence.csv")
collections = pd.read_csv(TALLY / "usage_by_collection.csv")
frame = pd.read_csv("../data/frame/frame.csv")

n_deposits = files["dataset_doi"].nunique()
n_files = len(files)
n_mentions = len(mentions)

# What the deposits say about the environment they ran in, with the
# denominator attached. Read without it, a count of deposits declaring Stata
# 14 reads as a census of a corpus in which seven deposits in eight say
# nothing at all.
environment = json.loads((TALLY / "environment_coverage.json").read_text())
n_stata_version = environment["stata_version"]["deposits_carrying"]
n_stata_version_of = environment["stata_version"]["deposits_eligible"]
n_r_version = environment["r_version"]["deposits_carrying"]
n_r_version_of = environment["r_version"]["deposits_eligible"]
share_stata_version = n_stata_version / n_stata_version_of
at_risk = (
    files[files["in_analysis_set"]]
    .groupby("language")["dataset_doi"]
    .nunique()
    .to_dict()
)

# A "mention" is not the same object across languages, so no total over all of
# them means anything. In R and Python a mention is an import statement; in
# Stata it is every command occurrence, because that is what a Stata program
# is, so a combined count would be a count of Stata's syntax.
#
# The comparable unit is a mention that *could* name a third-party package.
# That excludes Stata builtins, R and Python standard libraries, and programs
# defined inside the deposit -- none of which were ever candidates for registry
# resolution, so leaving them in the denominator deflates the unresolved rate
# by an order of magnitude -- both figures are computed below.
# It also excludes install and inquiry lines. `ssc install estout` states a
# dependency and is not a use, the headline tally already leaves it out, and
# counting it here measured the resolver on a population the paper reports
# nothing else about.
NOT_THIRD_PARTY = ("builtin", "base_or_stdlib", "local_program", "local_relative")
NON_USE = {str(c) for c in NON_USE_CONSTRUCTS}
uses = mentions[~mentions["construct"].isin(NON_USE)]
candidates = uses[~uses["resolution"].isin(NOT_THIRD_PARTY)]
mentions_by_language = mentions.groupby("language").size().to_dict()

# Computed, not typed. The naive rate is quoted in the text to show how much
# the denominator matters, so it has to move when the data does -- a stale
# literal there would be the same error the passage is about.
naive_unknown_share = mentions["resolution"].eq("unknown").mean()
stata_mentions_per_file = mentions_by_language.get("stata", 0) / max(
    1, files[files["language"] == "stata"]["file_uid"].nunique()
)
r_mentions_per_file = mentions_by_language.get("r", 0) / max(
    1, files[files["language"] == "r"]["file_uid"].nunique()
)
# The released index's own size, read from the index rather than typed, so the
# paper cannot disagree with the artifact it cites.
# Through the lock, so it is the index the tally was resolved against and not
# whichever copy happens to be on disk.
_lock = read_lock()
INDEX = pinned_directory("stata_index", _lock, payload=INDEX_FILE) / INDEX_FILE
# Counted as the released record counts them, so the paper and the deposit it
# cites print the same numbers: commands and packages excluding helper files,
# and packages per archive over every manifest the archive serves.
_index_all = con.execute(f"SELECT * FROM '{INDEX}'").df()
_commands = _index_all[~_index_all["is_helper"]]
n_index_packages = _commands["package"].nunique()
n_index_commands = _commands["command"].nunique()
index_by_source = _index_all.groupby("source")["package"].nunique().to_dict()
index = _index_all[_index_all.apply(credited, axis=1)]
n_ssc_packages = index_by_source.get("ssc", 0)
n_journal_packages = index_by_source.get("stata_journal", 0)
n_stb_packages = index_by_source.get("stb", 0)
n_net_packages = index_by_source.get("net", 0)
_net = _index_all[_index_all["source"] == "net"]
n_net_hosts = _net["issue"].nunique()
share_net_on_github = (
    _net[_net["issue"].str.contains("github")]["package"].nunique()
    / max(1, n_net_packages)
)
_index_source = json.loads((INDEX.parent / "source.json").read_text())
n_net_unreachable = len(_index_source.get("net_sites_unreachable", []))
# Quoted in Validation, so computed rather than typed.
n_stata_builtin_calls = int(
    (mentions["language"].eq("stata") & mentions["resolution"].eq("builtin")).sum()
)
# How much of the builtin list came from asking StataCorp rather than from
# curation. Read from the snapshot so it cannot drift from the artifact.
_verified = json.loads(
    Path("../registries/snapshots/stata_official/official.json").read_text()
)
# Against the *curated* list, not the shipped builtins.json -- that file is
# the merged set and already contains these names, so comparing to it returns
# zero and silently understates the whole point. This equals the official
# count because the crawl only asked about names that were unresolved or
# SSC-attributed; anything the curated list already knew was never queried.
# The SSC tier checked against a list compiled independently, by
# `scripts/validate_index.py`.
index_check = json.loads(Path("../build/validation/index_agreement.json").read_text())
n_base_ado = len(
    json.loads(
        (pinned_directory("stata_base_ado", _lock) / "names.json").read_text()
    )
)
n_verified_added = len(
    {n for n, ok in _verified["commands"].items() if ok} - set(curated().forms)
)
# The counterfactual quoted in Validation: what the unresolved rate would be
# with the curated list alone. It cannot be read off the tally -- it needs
# re-resolving -- so it is reconstructed rather than typed, which is the only
# way a comparison like this stays true after the next rebuild.
#
# Commands that are builtin only because the help server confirmed them rejoin
# the candidate pool. Those the SSC index also claims would have been credited
# to a package (the precision error); the rest would have read as unresolved.
_ssc_commands = {
    r[0]
    for r in con.execute(
        f"SELECT DISTINCT lower(command) FROM '{INDEX}' "
        "WHERE NOT is_helper AND source = 'ssc'"
    ).fetchall()
}
_readded = mentions[
    mentions["language"].eq("stata")
    & mentions["resolution"].eq("builtin")
    & ~mentions["normalized_name"].isin(set(curated().forms))
]
n_misattributed = int(_readded["normalized_name"].isin(_ssc_commands).sum())
curated_only_share = (
    candidates["resolution"].eq("unknown").sum() + len(_readded) - n_misattributed
) / (len(candidates) + len(_readded))

# Evidence for the archive-cap limitation: do bigger archives just hold more
# data, or more code too? Joined from the ledger, because the archives
# themselves are deleted after extraction.
#
# This was carried as a typed literal ("21 files to 221") measured on an
# earlier, smaller corpus. Recomputed here it is 13 to 41 -- the direction
# survives, the magnitude did not, which is the argument for computing it.
_ledger = {}
for _line in Path("../corpus/zenodo/ledger.jsonl").read_text().splitlines():
    if _line.strip():
        _r = json.loads(_line)
        _ledger["zenodo:" + _r["dataset_doi"].rsplit(".", 1)[-1]] = _r
_per_deposit = files.groupby("dataset_doi").size()
_sized = sorted(
    (_ledger[d]["bytes_fetched"], n)
    for d, n in _per_deposit.items()
    if d in _ledger and (_ledger[d].get("bytes_fetched") or 0) > 0
)
_q = max(1, len(_sized) // 4)
code_files_smallest = int(pd.Series([n for _, n in _sized[:_q]]).median())
code_files_largest = int(pd.Series([n for _, n in _sized[3 * _q :]]).median())

# Deposit-level coverage, by reason. A deposit that yielded nothing is not a
# finding about the deposit until you can say why, and the reasons are not
# interchangeable: an over-cap archive is a policy choice we made, a spanned
# archive is a format we declined to reassemble, and a failure is a bug or an
# outage. Reported as a table rather than one "coverage" number, because
# collapsing them lets a bug hide inside a stated limitation.
#
# Read from the ledger alone. The first version of this asked which deposits
# were absent from `files.parquet` and labeled the remainder "no code files
# in the deposit" -- which quietly counted 99 deposits collected after the
# tally was last built, plus 136 records that are not outcomes at all but
# requeue markers left by an earlier cap raise, carrying no counts and only
# surviving because the ledger takes the last write for a DOI. Comparing two
# artifacts built at different times measures the interval between them; the
# ledger is internally consistent, so it is the one to ask.
_last = {}
for _line in Path("../corpus/zenodo/ledger.jsonl").read_text().splitlines():
    if _line.strip():
        _r = json.loads(_line)
        _last[_r["dataset_doi"]] = _r
_reason_of = (
    ("n_skipped_over_cap", "archive over the size cap"),
    ("n_spanned", "multi-part archive, not reassembled"),
    ("n_failed", "download or extraction failed"),
)
_gaps = []
for _r in _last.values():
    if "n_candidate" not in _r:
        _gaps.append("awaiting re-collection")
        continue
    if _r["n_fetched"]:
        continue
    _why = next(
        (label for key, label in _reason_of if _r.get(key)),
        "deposit contains no code files",
    )
    _gaps.append(_why)
coverage = (
    pd.Series(_gaps).value_counts().rename_axis("reason").reset_index(name="deposits")
)
n_deposits_declared = len(_last)
n_deposits_collected = len(_last) - len(_gaps)
share_collected = n_deposits_collected / len(_last)
n_spanned_deposits = sum(1 for _r in _last.values() if _r.get("n_spanned"))

# The findings paragraphs. Every claim there is a computation here, including
# the qualitative one: which of the top Stata packages are exhibit preparation tools
# is a fixed, checkable list of names, not a judgment made at writing time.
# `presence` is per (source, language) now that both repositories go through
# one tally, so the headline counts sum across sources and the disciplinary
# comparison indexes into them rather than reading a second file.
_at_risk = presence.groupby("language")["n_deposits"].sum().to_dict()
n_stata_deposits = int(_at_risk.get("stata", 0))
n_r_deposits = int(_at_risk.get("r", 0))
n_python_deposits = int(_at_risk.get("python", 0))
stata_to_r_ratio = n_stata_deposits / max(1, n_r_deposits)

# The composition behind every pooled count in the paper.
_analyzable = files[files["in_analysis_set"]]
_by_source = _analyzable.groupby("source")["dataset_doi"].nunique()
n_zenodo_deposits = int(_by_source.get("zenodo", 0))
n_dataverse_deposits = int(_by_source.get("dataverse", 0))
n_deposits_analyzable = int(_analyzable["dataset_doi"].nunique())
n_collections_tallied = int(files["collection_id"].nunique())


def _top(language: str, n: int = 10):
    return usage[usage["language"] == language].nlargest(n, "n_deposits")


_top_stata = _top("stata")
n_top_stata = len(_top_stata)
top_stata_package = f"`{_top_stata.iloc[0]['package']}`"
top_stata_share = float(_top_stata.iloc[0]["share_of_deposits"])
_top_python = _top("python")
top_python_package = f"`{_top_python.iloc[0]['package']}`"
top_python_share = float(_top_python.iloc[0]["share_of_deposits"])

#: Stata packages whose purpose is formatting results for publication rather
#: than estimating anything. Named explicitly so the claim is falsifiable: a
#: reader can disagree with the membership of this set and recompute.
TABLE_MAKERS = {
    "estout",
    "outreg2",
    "coefplot",
    "tabout",
    "asdoc",
    "outtable",
    "esttab",
    "mktab",
    "xml_tab",
    "logout",
    "putexcel",
    "outreg",
}
_found_makers = [p for p in _top_stata["package"] if p in TABLE_MAKERS]
n_table_makers = len(_found_makers)
table_makers_list = ", ".join(f"`{p}`" for p in _found_makers)

#: Journal collections whose subject is economics. Named rather than read off
#: the repository, because that is exactly the confound the per-journal table
#: exists to rule out: five of these sit in Harvard Dataverse alongside the
#: political science journals, so if the split followed the repository they
#: would side with their neighbours. A reader who disagrees with a membership
#: here can change it and recompute.
ECONOMICS_COLLECTIONS = {
    "ej-replication-repository",
    "restud-replication",
    "es-replication-repository",
    "jeea_replication",
    "ectj-replication-repository",
    "restat",
    "qje",
    "JAERE",
    "rfs",
    "JPE",
}

# Deposits per collection containing analyzable Stata: the denominator the
# per-collection shares need, which the usage table cannot supply because it
# counts packages rather than collections.
_stata_deposits = (
    files[files["in_analysis_set"] & files["language"].eq("stata")]
    .groupby("collection_id")["dataset_doi"]
    .nunique()
)
_stata_by_collection = collections[collections["language"] == "stata"]
_biggest = _stata_deposits.nlargest(12).index

_rows = []
for _cid in _biggest:
    _here = _stata_by_collection[_stata_by_collection["collection_id"] == _cid]
    _ranked = _here.nlargest(3, "n_deposits")
    _rows.append(
        {
            "collection": _cid,
            "field": (
                "economics" if _cid in ECONOMICS_COLLECTIONS else "political science"
            ),
            "deposits": int(_stata_deposits[_cid]),
            **{
                f"#{i + 1}": f"{r.package} ({int(r.n_deposits)})"
                for i, r in enumerate(_ranked.itertuples())
            },
        }
    )
by_collection = pd.DataFrame(_rows)

# The claims, computed over every collection large enough to rank rather
# than over the twelve the table shows. The table illustrates; the statistic
# is the evidence, and restricting it to what fits on a page would be
# choosing the sample after seeing it.
MIN_STATA_DEPOSITS = 50

n_collections_shown = len(by_collection)
n_estout_first = int(by_collection["#1"].str.startswith("estout").sum())

_eligible = [
    c for c in _stata_deposits[_stata_deposits >= MIN_STATA_DEPOSITS].index
    if c in set(_stata_by_collection["collection_id"])
]


def _leans(collection_id: str) -> str:
    here = _stata_by_collection[_stata_by_collection["collection_id"] == collection_id]

    def loaded(package: str) -> int:
        return int(here.loc[here["package"] == package, "n_deposits"].sum())

    return "reghdfe" if loaded("reghdfe") > loaded("coefplot") else "coefplot"


_econ = [c for c in _eligible if c in ECONOMICS_COLLECTIONS]
_polsci = [c for c in _eligible if c not in ECONOMICS_COLLECTIONS]
n_ranked_collections = len(_eligible)
n_econ_shown = len(_econ)
n_polsci_shown = len(_polsci)
n_econ_reghdfe = sum(1 for c in _econ if _leans(c) == "reghdfe")
n_polsci_coefplot = sum(1 for c in _polsci if _leans(c) == "coefplot")

# The confound this rules out: economics journals that live in the Dataverse
# half, so repository is held constant and the split still appears.
_dv = set(files[files["source"].eq("dataverse")]["collection_id"])
n_econ_in_dataverse = sum(1 for c in _econ if c in _dv)

# The unresolved rate per *deposit*, which is the unit this paper argues for
# everywhere else and then quietly abandoned here. Pooling over mentions lets
# one deposit speak for the corpus, and one did until vendored library trees
# stopped being read as research code -- a deposit shipping a copy of Stata's
# `ado/base` contributed 46% of all unresolved Stata mentions by itself.
_per_deposit = (
    candidates.assign(unresolved=candidates["resolution"].eq("unknown"))
    .groupby("dataset_doi")["unresolved"]
    .agg(["size", "sum"])
)
_per_deposit["rate"] = _per_deposit["sum"] / _per_deposit["size"]
median_deposit_unresolved = float(_per_deposit["rate"].median())
p90_deposit_unresolved = float(_per_deposit["rate"].quantile(0.9))
share_deposits_fully_resolved = float((_per_deposit["sum"] == 0).mean())

# Validated use against the registries' own download counts. The counts are
# pinned snapshots like the registries, the table is built by
# `softverse.build.downloads`, and everything quoted is read off it.
versus = pd.read_csv(TALLY / "downloads_vs_use.csv")
agree = agreement(read_versus(TALLY / "downloads_vs_use.csv"))
REGISTRY_NAME = {"ssc": "Stata (SSC)", "cran": "R (CRAN)", "pypi": "Python (PyPI)"}
agreement_table = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {
            "registry": REGISTRY_NAME[e],
            "used": f"{a['used']['n']:,}",
            "rho, used": f"{a['used']['rho']:.2f}",
            "in 20 or more": f"{a['used']['rho_20']:.2f}",
            "counted": f"{a['registry']['n']:,}",
            "ever used": f"{a['registry']['ever_used']:.0%}",
            "rho, counted": f"{a['registry']['rho']:.2f}",
            "top 100 used": f"{a['registry']['top100_used']}",
        }
        for e, a in agree.items()
    ]
)
# Ranks among the packages the corpus uses, which is the population the
# sentence that quotes them is about.
_used = versus[versus["n_deposits"].gt(0) & versus["downloads"].notna()].copy()
_used["rank_by_use"] = _used.groupby("ecosystem")["n_deposits"].rank(
    ascending=False, method="min"
)
_used["rank_by_downloads"] = _used.groupby("ecosystem")["downloads"].rank(
    ascending=False, method="min"
)
_cran = agree["cran"]
_deps = _cran["dependencies"]


def _download_rank(package: str, ecosystem: str) -> int:
    row = _used[_used["package"].eq(package) & _used["ecosystem"].eq(ecosystem)]
    return int(row["rank_by_downloads"].iloc[0])


def _use_rank(package: str, ecosystem: str) -> int:
    row = _used[_used["package"].eq(package) & _used["ecosystem"].eq(ecosystem)]
    return int(row["rank_by_use"].iloc[0])


def _furthest(ecosystem: str, *, above: bool, n: int = 4) -> str:
    """The packages ranked furthest above, or below, their download rank.

    Among packages in at least five deposits, the same rule the figure labels
    by, so the prose names what the figure shows and both move together.
    """
    d = versus[
        versus["ecosystem"].eq(ecosystem)
        & versus["downloads"].gt(0)
        & versus["n_deposits"].ge(5)
    ].copy()
    # Among packages in at least five deposits, so an unused package, which
    # the table now carries too, is never named as "over-ranked".
    d["gap"] = d["downloads"].rank(ascending=False) - d["n_deposits"].rank(ascending=False)
    picked = d.nlargest(n, "gap") if above else d.nsmallest(n, "gap")
    names = [f"`{p}`" for p in picked["package"]]
    return ", ".join(names[:-1]) + " and " + names[-1]


def ordinal(n: int) -> str:
    """`4th`, `281st`: a rank as a reader says it."""
    suffix = "th" if n % 100 in (11, 12, 13) else {1: "st", 2: "nd", 3: "rd"}.get(n % 10, "th")
    return f"{n:,}{suffix}"


n_pypi_counted = agree["pypi"]["registry"]["n"]

# Where the software a deposit uses lives, per language and per deposit. The
# registry a language is known by is one place among several, and which others
# matter differs by language -- which is the finding, so it is computed for
# all three rather than asserted for one.
LOCATIONS = {
    "cran": "primary registry",
    "pypi": "primary registry",
    "ssc": "primary registry",
    "bioconductor": "secondary archive",
    "cran_archive": "secondary archive",
    "stata_journal": "secondary archive",
    "stb": "secondary archive",
    "github": "code host",
    "gitlab": "code host",
    "bitbucket": "code host",
    "net_site": "author's site",
}
LOCATION_ORDER = [
    "primary registry",
    "secondary archive",
    "code host",
    "author's site",
    "unresolved",
]
_located = candidates.assign(
    location=candidates["ecosystem"].map(LOCATIONS).where(
        ~candidates["resolution"].eq("unknown"), "unresolved"
    )
).dropna(subset=["location"])
_at_risk = _located.groupby("language")["dataset_doi"].nunique()
_in_location = (
    _located.groupby(["language", "location"])["dataset_doi"].nunique().unstack(fill_value=0)
)
location_share = _in_location.div(_at_risk, axis=0).reindex(columns=LOCATION_ORDER, fill_value=0)
where_software_lives = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {
            "language": {"stata": "Stata", "r": "R", "python": "Python"}[language],
            "deposits": f"{_at_risk[language]:,}",
            **{c: f"{location_share.loc[language, c]:.1%}" for c in LOCATION_ORDER},
        }
        for language in ("stata", "r", "python")
    ]
)
share_stata_secondary = float(location_share.loc["stata", "secondary archive"])
share_stata_net = float(location_share.loc["stata", "author's site"])
share_r_code_host = float(location_share.loc["r", "code host"])
share_r_secondary = float(location_share.loc["r", "secondary archive"])
share_r_archived = (
    _located[_located["ecosystem"].eq("cran_archive")]["dataset_doi"].nunique()
    / _at_risk["r"]
)
share_unresolved = location_share["unresolved"].to_dict()
n_stata_beyond_ssc = int(
    _located[
        _located["language"].eq("stata")
        & _located["location"].isin(["secondary archive", "author's site"])
    ]["dataset_doi"].nunique()
)
n_stata_beyond_ssc_packages = int(
    _located[
        _located["language"].eq("stata")
        & _located["location"].isin(["secondary archive", "author's site"])
    ]["resolved_package"].nunique()
)

# A remote install vouches for a name only inside its own deposit. The looser
# rule -- the corpus installs this name from a code host *somewhere* -- is
# reported beside it rather than applied, so a reader can see what it would add.
_hosted = set(
    mentions[mentions["ecosystem"].isin(["github", "gitlab", "bitbucket"])]["raw_name"]
)
_r_unknown = candidates[
    candidates["language"].eq("r") & candidates["resolution"].eq("unknown")
]
n_r_hosted_elsewhere_deposits = int(
    _r_unknown[_r_unknown["raw_name"].isin(_hosted)]["dataset_doi"].nunique()
)
n_r_unknown_deposits = int(_r_unknown["dataset_doi"].nunique())

# What is left, labeled by hand. Every name used in at least this many
# deposits that nothing above accounts for was looked up and given a category,
# and the file is released; the threshold is where the list stops being
# software and becomes typos and one deposit's own helpers.
residue = pd.read_csv("../data/validation/unregistered_labelled.csv")
if residue["category"].isna().any():
    raise ValueError("unregistered_labelled.csv has unlabelled rows")
RESIDUE_MIN_DEPOSITS = int(residue["n_deposits"].min())
SOFTWARE_CATEGORIES = [
    "formal archive not indexed",
    "code host",
    "author site",
    "commercial",
    "unidentified",
]
residue_table = (
    residue.sort_values("n_deposits", ascending=False)
    .groupby("category")
    .agg(
        names=("name", "size"),
        **{"most used": ("name", lambda n: ", ".join(n[:3]))},
    )
    .reindex(
        [*SOFTWARE_CATEGORIES, "official, undocumented", "local program", "not software"]
    )
    .dropna()
    .reset_index()
)
residue_table["names"] = residue_table["names"].astype(int)
n_residue_names = len(residue)
n_residue_software = int(residue["category"].isin(SOFTWARE_CATEGORIES).sum())
n_residue_not_software = n_residue_names - n_residue_software

# Named in Validation. The most *widespread* unresolved Stata name, ranked by
# deposits rather than mentions: one deposit calling something six hundred
# times is one user of it, and a mention-ranked list is a ranking of whichever
# deposits are largest.
_stata_unknown = candidates[
    candidates["language"].eq("stata") & candidates["resolution"].eq("unknown")
]
_by_deposits = _stata_unknown.groupby("normalized_name")["dataset_doi"].nunique()
top_unresolved_stata = f"`{_by_deposits.idxmax()}`"
n_top_unresolved_deposits = int(_by_deposits.max())
n_unresolved_stata_names = len(_by_deposits)
n_unresolved_stata_singletons = int((_by_deposits == 1).sum())
stata_unknown_share_of_all = len(_stata_unknown) / max(
    1, int(candidates["resolution"].eq("unknown").sum())
)

# The two categories that exist so that "we cannot name a package" is not
# confused with "there is no package here". Both were folded into `unknown`
# until the construct was allowed to reach the resolver.
n_local_relative = int(mentions["resolution"].eq("local_relative").sum())
n_dynamic = int(mentions["resolution"].eq("dynamic").sum())

# R's own parser as a true oracle for the syntactic task. Unlike the `renv`
# comparison below this is not a peer agreement: R's parser defines the
# answer, so disagreement is our error and the rate is exact.
_oracle = json.loads(Path("../build/validation/r_oracle.json").read_text())
n_oracle_files = _oracle["n_files_compared"]
n_oracle_unparseable = _oracle["n_files_unparseable_by_r"]
n_oracle_pairs = _oracle["true_positives"] + _oracle["false_negatives"]
oracle_precision = _oracle["precision"]
oracle_recall = _oracle["recall"]
# Per source, because until recently this check globbed the Zenodo directory
# and reported its result as though it described the corpus.
n_oracle_sources = len(_oracle["by_source"])
n_oracle_dataverse_files = _oracle["by_source"]["dataverse"]["n_files_compared"]

# Cross-tool agreement, read from the artifact `scripts/validate_renv.py`
# writes. This paragraph used to carry a typed 0.998 that nothing in the
# repository computed -- no script, no artifact, no recorded run. It was the
# one number here with no provenance at all, and it was wrong by about a
# tenth; the check that caught it is `tests/test_paper.py`, which fails on any
# bare numeral left in the prose.
_renv = json.loads(Path("../build/validation/renv_agreement.json").read_text())

# The reachability bound, from `scripts/reachability.py`. Promised by an
# earlier draft and never computed: the schema carried an `is_reachable`
# column written as null. It is computed now, and what it does to the ranking
# is reported below whether or not it flatters the measure.
_reach = json.loads(Path("../build/validation/reachability.json").read_text())
n_graph_complete = _reach["n_deposits_complete"]
n_graph_master = _reach["n_deposits_with_master"]
n_graph_considered = _reach["n_deposits_considered"]
share_files_reachable = _reach["complete"]["share_reachable"]
median_share_reachable = _reach["complete"]["median_share_reachable"]
n_macro_edges = _reach["n_macro_edges"]
n_followed_edges = _reach["n_edges"]
reach_retained = {k: v["median_retained"] for k, v in _reach["usage"].items()}
reach_worst = {k: v["min_retained"] for k, v in _reach["usage"].items()}
max_rank_move = max(v["max_rank_move"] for v in _reach["usage"].values())
reach_table = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {
            "Language": {"stata": "Stata", "r": "R", "python": "Python"}[language],
            "Package": row["package"],
            "Deposits": row["n_deposits"],
            "Reached by a master": row["n_deposits_reachable_only"],
            "Kept": f"{row['retained']:.0%}",
            "Rank": f"{row['rank']} to {row['rank_reachable_only']}",
        }
        for language, block in _reach["usage"].items()
        for row in block["top"][:5]
    ]
)
n_renv_compared = _renv["n_deposits_compared"]
renv_mean_jaccard = _renv["mean_jaccard"]
renv_pooled_jaccard = _renv["pooled_jaccard"]
renv_perfect_share = _renv["n_perfect_agreement"] / _renv["n_deposits_compared"]
renv_version = _renv["renv_version"]
n_renv_unreadable = _renv["n_renv_read_nothing"]
# The direction of the residual disagreement. Summed over every disagreement
# rather than over the 50 worst, which the artifact also carries: selecting on
# lowest Jaccard selects for deposits where renv read almost nothing, and the
# tail leans the opposite way to the population it is drawn from.
n_renv_ours_only = _renv["n_ours_only"]
n_renv_theirs_only = _renv["n_renv_only"]
# What the aligned comparison set aside before scoring, and the score without
# setting it aside, so the adjustment is on the page rather than trusted.
_aside = _renv["set_aside"]
n_renv_aside_base = _aside.get("base_r", 0)
n_renv_aside_rmarkdown = _aside.get("implicit_rmarkdown", 0)
n_renv_aside_outside = _aside.get("outside_analysis_files", 0)
renv_raw_mean_jaccard = _renv["raw"]["mean_jaccard"]
renv_raw_pooled_jaccard = _renv["raw"]["pooled_jaccard"]

# Named in Limitations: Stata keywords reaching command position. Computed,
# so that closing one of the gaps shows up here rather than leaving a stale
# boast in the prose.
_keyword_noise = _stata_unknown[_stata_unknown["normalized_name"].isin(
    {"in", "using", "str"}
)]
n_keyword_noise = len(_keyword_noise)
n_keyword_noise_deposits = int(_keyword_noise["dataset_doi"].nunique())

# Named in Limitations. Computed so the claim cannot go stale silently.
# Written as a computed sentence rather than two typed package names, so a
# false positive that gets fixed disappears from the prose instead of being
# reported as affecting zero deposits. `wordy` did exactly that once vendored
# library code stopped being read as research code.
_KNOWN_FALSE_POSITIVES = {"fastcd": "c", "wordy": "word"}
_residual = {
    pkg: int(
        mentions[
            (mentions["language"] == "stata") & (mentions["resolved_package"] == pkg)
        ]["dataset_doi"].nunique()
    )
    for pkg in _KNOWN_FALSE_POSITIVES
}
residual_false_positives = (
    ", ".join(
        f"`{pkg}` (command `{_KNOWN_FALSE_POSITIVES[pkg]}`) in {n} deposits"
        for pkg, n in sorted(_residual.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])
        if n
    )
    or "none"
)
stata_builtin_share = (
    mentions[mentions["language"] == "stata"]["resolution"].eq("builtin").mean()
)
```

Research software earns its authors little credit [@howison2011; @smith2016]. A hiring committee knows what a paper is worth and not what a package is worth, so useful software goes unwritten [@sood_countpy]. Part of the problem is the count. The usual measure of how much a package is used is how often it is downloaded, and a download costs almost nothing to produce. This paper proposes a count that is expensive to move, whether a package is loaded in the replication code a journal requires and checks, and compares it with downloads in `{python} f"{n_deposits_analyzable:,}"` deposits from economics and political science journals. The two disagree most about the packages that matter. Among R packages used in at least twenty deposits, the rank correlation is `{python} f"{agree['cran']['used']['rho_20']:.2f}"`, and `stargazer`, the `{python} ordinal(_use_rank("stargazer", "cran"))` most used, is the `{python} ordinal(_download_rank("stargazer", "cran"))` most downloaded.

A count used to give credit is a signal, and a signal is worth what it costs to produce [@spence1973]. A build server that installs a package on every commit produces hundreds of downloads, a mirror produces more, and a maintainer who releases more often collects more again [@sood_countpy]. PyPI's own operators found in 2026 that metadata requests were a large share of the downloads of widely installed packages, and that much of the rest came from misconfigured proxies and runaway build systems [@pypi2026downloads]. A mention in prose is one sentence in a methods section [@schindler2022], and often the sentence is missing: in biology, between a third and a half of software mentions are formal citations, and the version is usually lost [@howison2016software].

Deposited code is not cheap. Economics and political science journals ask authors to deposit the code behind an accepted paper, and some run it before publication [@stodden2018; @vilhuber2020; @herbert2024reproduce]. To add one to a package's count there, someone has to get a paper accepted at such a journal with the package loaded in its code. I call a package's appearance in that code **validated use**.

The cost is what separates this count from two I built before it. In 2018 I counted how often public GitHub repositories import each Python package [@sood2018countpy], and in 2025 I estimated the same from a random sample of repositories [@sood2025user]. Both count use rather than fetches, and both share a weaker form of the defect in downloads: anyone can push a repository. Nobody can move a count over verified deposits without publishing a paper.[^priority]

[^priority]: I proposed counting package use in code instead of downloads in March 2019 [@sood_countpy]. The first version of this collector, which read imports out of *Journal of Politics* Dataverse deposits, was committed in July 2023 [@sood2023softverse]. It lacked a sampling frame, validation, an index for Stata and a released corpus. This paper supplies them.

I measure validated use in R, Python and Stata across `{python} f"{n_deposits_analyzable:,}"` deposits from `{python} f"{n_collections_tallied:,}"` journal collections, and ask three questions:

1. **RQ1 (Validity of usage metrics):** How far do validated use and download counts agree, and which software does each overstate?
2. **RQ2 (Registries as instruments):** What does counting through a package registry leave out, in each language, and where does the missing software live?
3. **RQ3 (Field-specific dependence):** Which software does each field depend on?

The paper adds two things to the counts. One is the measurement: a sampling frame, a validated extractor for three languages, and the mention-level record, released so the counts can be recomputed. The other is an index from Stata commands to the packages that provide them, built from the distribution manifests of SSC, the *Stata Journal*, the *Stata Technical Bulletin* and the authors' sites that replication code installs from. Sergio Correia compiled such a list for SSC alone, for the AEA Data Editor's package scanner [@reiner2021packagesearch]. Nothing covered the other three archives, and `grc1leg`, one of the most used Stata packages in this corpus, lives in none of the lists an SSC index can hold.

## Related work

### How the use of research software has been measured

Most of what is known comes from reading papers. In a hand-coded sample of ninety biology articles, most software mentions were informal, a minority were formal citations, and the software mentioned was often impossible to find or to pin to a version [@howison2016software]. Later work automated the reading. Nearly five thousand PDFs in biomedicine and economics were annotated by hand to train extractors [@du2021softcite]; one such extractor was run over PubMed Central and its output built into a knowledge graph [@schindler2022]; the mentions in the biomedical literature were released at scale [@istrate2022czsoftware]. The same pipeline shows citation practice improving slowly in the coronavirus literature [@du2022cord19] and shows retracted articles using less open-source software than matched controls [@schindler2023retracted].

Citation counts of software are the second instrument, and the studies that use them mostly document why they fail. Software is rarely cited in the databases built to index research outputs [@park2019software]. One widely used R package is cited under many inconsistent forms [@li2019lme4], and the citation formats R packages ask for change over a package's life [@wang2024rcitation]. Institutional repositories hold very little software as a recognized output [@carlin2023where].

All of these read what authors wrote about software. This paper reads the software they ran, which removes the step at which a use goes unrecorded. Three efforts have read code before. One executed the R files in over 2,000 Harvard Dataverse deposits to ask whether they ran [@trisovic2022]. One had students inspect the replication files of more than ten thousand economics, political science and statistics papers and record which *language* each used [@upton2026software], and another classified economics replication packages by file extension to the same end [@kranz2023usage]. One resolved SSC package names out of economics replication code, to validate a Stata command that pins package versions, and found that the hundred most downloaded packages are 71% of SSC downloads but 93% of the packages publications load [@correia2024require]. None publishes per-package counts across languages with the denominator each share divides by. Two unpublished efforts come close: `renv` run over R scripts in Dataverse deposits [@arelbundock2022which], and the AEA Data Editor's scan of do-files for SSC packages during review [@aeadataeditor2021statapackagesearch; @reiner2021packagesearch]. Downloads remain the standing answer to how much a Stata command is used [@choodari2016uptake].

### What a count is for

The case that software work is under-rewarded is older than these measurements. Scientists write software inside a reputation system that pays in publications and citations, which shapes what gets written and whether it is maintained [@howison2011], and most learn to write it from peers rather than from training [@hannay2009scientists]. A review of what funders, maintainers and scientists would need to measure, from funding through use to scientific impact, found few measures of use [@howison2015ecosystem]. The software citation principles are the normative answer: cite software as one cites a paper [@smith2016]. A recent study paired articles with their code repositories and found that a large share have code contributors who are not authors [@brown2026code]. It measures who wrote the code behind a paper; this paper measures whose code the paper's analysis ran on.

A count that gives credit will be gamed if it can be. Citation counts are inflated through reference metadata that never appears in the article [@besancon2024sneaked], and researchers choosing what to read respond to whichever indicators are put in front of them [@lemke2021conjoint]. So the question to ask of any count is what it costs to move. This paper asks it of downloads and of its own measure.

## What validated use means

The estimand:

> Among replication deposits in collection *J* containing at least one
> analyzable script in language *L*, the share that statically reference
> package *P*.

The unit is the deposit, not the mention. A deposit that calls `ggplot2` two
hundred times is one user of `ggplot2`. A count weighted by mentions would
rank the largest deposits.

A static reference is not a run. A deposit may load a package in an old
script, in a branch that never executes, or in setup code that never runs,
and code left out of the deposit cannot be seen at all. A replication package
is a curated artifact, not a copy of the environment that produced the paper
[@trisovic2022]. Where a deposit has a master script, the counts can be
recomputed over the files it reaches, and the ranking holds.[^reach]

[^reach]: In the `{python} f"{n_graph_complete:,}"` deposits whose master
script's calls can all be followed, the median deposit has
`{python} f"{median_share_reachable:.0%}"` of its files on that path, and
recomputing over reachable files moves no package among the twenty most used
by more than `{python} f"{max_rank_move}"` places. The appendix has the
details.

A reference also means a direct one. A deposit that loads `fixest` also runs
`Rcpp` and `sandwich`, and neither is counted. What an author chose and what
the choice pulled in are different quantities, and crediting the closure
would put whatever popular packages depend on at the top of the table.

The closure could be added for two of the three languages. R declares
dependencies in `DESCRIPTION` and Python in a distribution's `requires_dist`,
and both can be walked by machine. An SSC `.pkg` manifest records them, when
it records them at all, as prose: the `reghdfe` manifest reads
`Requires: Stata version 11.2 and ftools from SSC (q.v.)`.

## Methods

### Sampling frame

```{python}
#| label: frame-table
located = frame[frame["collection_id"].notna() & (frame["collection_id"] != "")]
zen = located[located["source"] == "zenodo"]
unlocated = frame[frame["notes"].fillna("").str.startswith("unlocated")]

# The Dataverse half of the frame, enumerated collection by collection rather
# than declared: one request returns a journal's whole dataset list, so these
# are counted deposits and not an estimate.
_dv_path = Path("../data/frame/dataverse_deposits.csv")
dv = pd.read_csv(_dv_path) if _dv_path.exists() else pd.DataFrame()
n_dv_deposits = len(dv)
n_dv_collections = dv["collection_id"].nunique() if len(dv) else 0
n_frame_total = int(zen["n_records_declared"].sum()) + n_dv_deposits
```

The frame is the list of journals whose data-and-code policy the Social
Science Data Editors *actively verify*, from their Data and Code Availability
Standard. The frame spans two repositories because the two hold different
disciplines: Zenodo's verified collections are economics journals, and
Harvard Dataverse's journal collections are mostly political science. The
first appendix lists the collections.


Each Dataverse collection's deposits were listed in full through the
repository's API, paging where a collection exceeded one page, so the counts
are enumerated and not taken from the repository's own figures. One
collection present in a 2024 snapshot, `regionalstatistics`, no longer exists.
Six collections returned nothing on a first pass; five of them answered
minutes later and were retried, and the sixth is the one that is gone.

`{python} len(unlocated)` journals on the list are recorded as **unlocated**:
eight AEA titles deposit to openICPSR, which this corpus does not cover, and
two could not be placed. Every Zenodo community slug was checked before use,
because Zenodo ignores an unknown `communities=` filter and returns all 7.1
million records.


Of `{python} f"{n_deposits_declared:,}"` Zenodo deposits attempted,
`{python} f"{n_deposits_collected:,}"`
(`{python} f"{share_collected:.0%}"`) yielded files. \Cref{tab:coverage}, in
the first appendix, gives the reason for each of the rest: an archive over the
size cap, a multi-part archive that was not reassembled, or a download that
failed.


### Measurement


Strings and comments are excluded by structure. In a syntax tree,
`cat("run library(dplyr)")` is a call whose argument is a string node, so a
walk over call nodes never sees the text inside it. Regular expressions give
no such guarantee, and the appendix measures the difference.

Stata needed an index. R has CRAN and Python has PyPI, so an import can be
looked up. Stata has no registry that maps a command to its package, so the
mapping was rebuilt from distribution manifests:
`{python} f"{n_index_packages:,}"` packages and
`{python} f"{n_index_commands:,}"` commands across four kinds of archive,
released with this paper.

One such list already existed for SSC. Sergio Correia compiled a
command-to-package list for the AEA Data Editor's package scanner
[@reiner2021packagesearch], by a route that shares no code with the crawl
here. The two lists hold `{python} f"{index_check['n_shared']:,}"` commands in
common and name the same package for
`{python} f"{index_check['n_same_package']:,}"` of them. The crawl holds
`{python} f"{index_check['n_only_ours']:,}"` SSC commands that list lacks and
lacks `{python} f"{index_check['n_only_theirs']:,}"` it holds, most of them
internal subroutines.

A manifest lists the files a package ships, which is not the list of commands
it provides. Two rules close the gap. A file named by Stata's convention for
internal subroutines, such as `_eststo` or `reghdfe_p`, is a helper: a call to
it counts as a use of its package, and it is not reported as a command of its
own. A journal package is credited with a command only when it also ships
that command's help file, because an article's package bundles whatever its
example needs; a *Stata Journal* package for calibrating Cox models ships a
copy of `grc1leg.ado`. A command found in more than one archive is credited
to the first of SSC, the *Journal*, the *Bulletin* and the authors' sites to
list it, since journal authors mirror their software to SSC.

One kind of package has no command to find. `egen n = nvals(x)` calls
official `egen`, which runs a file named `_gnvals.ado`, and a package such as
`egenmore` is a collection of such files. Each `egen` call is therefore read
twice, as the command and as the file its function lives in, and the file
resolves to official Stata where Stata ships it and to its package where a
package does.

The download counts are existing data. SSC's are the monthly hits behind
Stata's `ssc hot`, served by RePEc. CRAN's come from one mirror's logs through
`cranlogs` [@csardi2015cranlogs]. PyPI's are a monthly dump of its public
download table for the fifteen thousand most downloaded projects
[@vankemenade2026toppypi]. Each is pinned by date and digest beside the
registries.

Shares are not comparable across languages. `{python} top_python_package`
appears in `{python} f"{top_python_share:.0%}"` of Python deposits because
Python in a replication package almost always means a dataframe pipeline.
Stata's most used package reaches `{python} f"{top_stata_share:.0%}"` over a
much longer tail, because Stata does natively what a Python deposit imports a
library to do. The two are shares of different kinds of deposit.

## Results

```{python}
#| label: top-packages
rows = []
for lang in ("stata", "r", "python"):
    top = usage[usage["language"] == lang].nlargest(10, "n_deposits")
    for _, r in top.iterrows():
        rows.append({
            "language": lang,
            "package": r["package"],
            "deposits": int(r["n_deposits"]),
            "of": int(r["n_deposits_at_risk"]),
            "share": f"{r['share_of_deposits']:.0%}",
        })
_top = pd.DataFrame(rows)
_top.columns = ["language", "package", "deposits", "of", "share"]
table(
    _top,
    caption="Most used third-party packages, by language",
    label="tab:top-packages",
    note=(
        "The ten packages appearing in the most deposits in each language. "
        "\\emph{deposits} counts deposits referencing the package; "
        "\\emph{of} is the number of deposits containing analyzable code in "
        "that language, and the share divides by it. A deposit counts once "
        "however many times it calls the package."
    ),
)
```

Every count pools both repositories: `{python} f"{n_zenodo_deposits:,}"`
deposits of economics from Zenodo and
`{python} f"{n_dataverse_deposits:,}"` of political science from Harvard
Dataverse, across `{python} f"{n_collections_tallied:,}"` collections. The
released table carries the split beside every pooled total, because the two
halves differ in size.

Every count is a share of the deposits **at risk**: those that contain
analyzable code in the language. A deposit counts as at risk for a language
when it holds an analyzable file in that language or when a reference in that
language came out of it. The second clause covers notebooks and literate
documents, whose file type is `ipynb` or `Rmd` while the code inside is
Python or R; without it a deposit whose only Python lives in a notebook would
enter the numerator of every Python package it loads and the denominator of
none.

### What published code loads

```{python}
#| label: fig-credit
figure(
    "figures/credit.pdf",
    caption="The twelve most used Stata packages, by share of deposits",
    label="fig:credit",
    note=(
        "Packages whose purpose is presenting results rather than estimating "
        "anything are filled dark. Counts to the right of each bar are "

    ),
)
```

Of the ten most used Stata packages (\cref{tab:top-packages}),
`{python} f"{n_table_makers:,}"` prepare exhibits and estimate nothing:
`{python} table_makers_list`. \cref{fig:credit} shows the same ordering with
those packages marked. The most used of all is `{python} top_stata_package`,
in `{python} f"{top_stata_share:.0%}"` of Stata deposits, ahead of every
regression command.

Much of what research depends on, then, is the machinery that turns estimates
into a publishable table or figure, and the field uses that machinery
constantly and cites it almost never.

```{python}
    "figures/reach.pdf",

    note=(
        "Packages the registry has a download count for, split into tenths by "
        "that count. For PyPI the tenths are of its fifteen thousand most "
        "downloaded projects."
    ),
)
```

The answer depends on which packages you ask about, so \cref{tab:agreement}
asks from both sides. Start from every package a registry counts. Downloads
then say a good deal about *whether* this field uses a package.
`{python} f"{agree['cran']['registry']['ever_used']:.0%}"` of CRAN appears in
any deposit; `{python} f"{agree['cran']['registry']['deciles'][-1]:.0%}"` of
its most downloaded tenth does, against
`{python} f"{agree['cran']['registry']['deciles'][0]:.0%}"` of its least
downloaded, and `{python} agree['cran']['registry']['top100_used']` of the
hundred most downloaded packages appear somewhere (\cref{fig:reach}). Now
start from the packages the field uses. Downloads say much less about *how
much*. Among R packages in at least twenty deposits, the ones a committee
would ask about, the rank correlation is
`{python} f"{agree['cran']['used']['rho_20']:.2f}"`. `stargazer` is
`{python} ordinal(_use_rank("stargazer", "cran"))` among R packages by
validated use and `{python} ordinal(_download_rank("stargazer", "cran"))` by
downloads.

The two counts disagree for two reasons, and only one bears on this paper's
argument. The first is that they count different people. Downloads pool
everyone who uses R or Python; this corpus is economics and political
science. `{python} _furthest("pypi", above=False)` rank far higher by
downloads than by use here partly because most Python is not written by
social scientists. Holding the audience fixed shows how much of the gap that
explains. Among the `{python} _cran['task_view']['n']` R packages the corpus
uses that CRAN's *Econometrics* and *Causal Inference* task views list, which
is software written for this field, the correlation rises from
`{python} f"{_cran['used']['rho']:.2f}"` to
`{python} f"{_cran['task_view']['rho']:.2f}"`.

The second reason is that a download is cheap, and it shows in what downloads
track. Across the R packages the corpus uses, downloads correlate at
`{python} f"{_deps['rho_downloads']:.2f}"` with the number of other packages
that install the package as a dependency; validated use correlates with that
number at `{python} f"{_deps['rho_use']:.2f}"`. Downloads come close to
measuring a package's place in the dependency graph. The R packages ranked
furthest below their download rank, `{python} _furthest("cran", above=False)`
(\cref{fig:downloads}), are all installed by other software, on every machine
and build server that installs the other software. Given a package's reverse
dependencies, downloads add a partial rank correlation of
`{python} f"{_deps['rho_partial']:.2f}"` with use.

One prediction failed. I expected agreement to rise once heavily depended-on
packages were set aside, at two cut-offs fixed in advance. It fell, to
`{python} f"{_deps['rho_at_most_100']:.2f}"` among packages with at most a
hundred reverse dependencies and `{python} f"{_deps['rho_at_most_10']:.2f}"`
with at most ten. The packages set aside are the head of both lists,
`ggplot2` and `dplyr`, where the two counts agree, and among packages nothing
depends on, downloads carry little signal of any kind. I computed the partial
correlation above after seeing that result, so it describes and does not test.

Agreement also falls as automatic installation rises across registries. It is
highest for Stata, `{python} f"{agree['ssc']['used']['rho']:.2f}"`, where
`{python} top_stata_package` leads both lists and a package is installed only
when a person types `ssc install`. It is lower for R, whose packages declare
dependencies that install with them, and lowest for Python,
`{python} f"{agree['pypi']['used']['rho']:.2f}"`, where continuous
integration reinstalls an environment on every commit. The costly-signal argument predicts this order. Three registries are three observations.

Concentration differs too. The hundred most downloaded CRAN packages take
`{python} f"{agree['cran']['registry']['top100_share_of_downloads']:.0%}"` of
CRAN's downloads and
`{python} f"{agree['cran']['registry']['top100_share_of_use']:.0%}"` of the
package uses in this corpus. For SSC the two shares are
`{python} f"{agree['ssc']['registry']['top100_share_of_downloads']:.0%}"` and
`{python} f"{agree['ssc']['registry']['top100_share_of_use']:.0%}"`, close to
each other and well below the 93% share of package loads that
@correia2024require report for economics code, on a different corpus in an
earlier month.

A download count exists only where a registry keeps one. Software the corpus
finds in the *Stata Journal*, the *Bulletin*, an author's site or a GitHub
repository has none. `{python} f"{agree['pypi']['used']['n_censored']:,}"` of
the Python packages the corpus uses fall below the
`{python} f"{n_pypi_counted:,}"` projects PyPI's counts cover, which tells us
one thing about them: each has fewer downloads than every project on that
list. Ranked as tied at the bottom, they move the Python correlation from
`{python} f"{agree['pypi']['used']['rho']:.2f}"` to
`{python} f"{agree['pypi']['used']['rho_censored']:.2f}"`.

### RQ2: What a registry leaves out

```{python}
#| label: fig-languages
figure(
    "figures/languages.pdf",
    caption="Languages by repository, and so by discipline",
    label="fig:languages",
    note=(
        "Share of deposits containing at least one analyzable file in each "
        "language. Zenodo's verified collections are economics journals; the "
        "Harvard Dataverse collections are mostly political science. A "
        "deposit may contain more than one language, so the bars within a "
        "repository do not sum to one hundred."
    ),
)
```

`{python} f"{n_stata_deposits:,}"` deposits contain analyzable Stata against
`{python} f"{n_r_deposits:,}"` with R and
`{python} f"{n_python_deposits:,}"` with Python, roughly
`{python} f"{stata_to_r_ratio:.1f}"` Stata deposits for every R one.
\cref{fig:languages} shows that the split follows discipline: economics
deposits are Stata, and political science deposits are mixed.

Studies of research software cover R and Python, the two languages with
public package registries. That leaves out the language most of this code is
written in, and it leaves it out because Stata is harder to count, so the
discipline that uses Stata most drops from the record for a reason unrelated
to how much software it uses. The next subsection measures what the
registries miss.

### Registries: what they cover and what they miss

```{python}
#| label: tbl-locations
table(
    where_software_lives,
    caption="Where the software a deposit uses lives",
    label="tab:locations",
    align="lrrrrrr",
    note=(
        "Share of deposits using at least one package found in each place, "
        "over deposits with any use that could name a third-party package; a "
        "deposit can appear in several columns. The primary registry is SSC, "
        "CRAN or PyPI. Secondary archives are the \\emph{Stata Journal} and "
        "the \\emph{Stata Technical Bulletin} for Stata, and Bioconductor and "
        "the CRAN archive for R. A code host is credited only when the deposit "
        "itself installs the package from one. \\emph{Unresolved} is a deposit "
        "using at least one name that none of these accounts for."
    ),
)
```

A package can be counted only if the name in the code can be looked up
somewhere. For R and Python one registry does almost all of that work. For
Stata no single registry does, and \cref{tab:locations} shows where the rest
of its software lives.

Stata's software is scattered, not informal. SSC holds
`{python} f"{n_ssc_packages:,}"` packages. The *Stata Journal* and its
predecessor, the *Stata Technical Bulletin*, publish the software behind their
articles: `{python} f"{n_journal_packages:,}"` and
`{python} f"{n_stb_packages:,}"` packages. Authors serve more from their own
sites; `grc1leg`, which combines graphs under one legend, comes from a
StataCorp developer's page and from nowhere else. All of these use the format
`net install` reads, a `stata.toc` listing packages and a `.pkg` manifest
listing each package's files, and none was indexed by command. I indexed all
four. `{python} f"{n_stata_beyond_ssc:,}"` deposits use at least one of the
`{python} f"{n_stata_beyond_ssc_packages:,}"` packages that an index of SSC
alone reports as belonging to nothing, among them `renvars`, published in the
*Bulletin*.

Authors' sites have no list, so they are found from the code. Every
`net install ..., from(URL)` line in the corpus names one, and each site named
is then crawled whole from its own `stata.toc`, because `net install` is
typed once by hand and most deposits that use a command carry no install line
for it. Looking up the names still unplaced led to three more sites, one of
them the new home of the SPost suite. Together that is
`{python} f"{n_net_packages:,}"` packages on `{python} f"{n_net_hosts:,}"`
hosts, `{python} f"{share_net_on_github:.0%}"` of them on GitHub, and
`{python} f"{n_net_unreachable}"` addresses that no longer serve a manifest.
A site no deposit installs from is not found. That bounds this tier by the
corpus in a way the other three are not.

Registries lose software as well as lacking it.
`{python} f"{share_r_archived:.0%}"` of R deposits load a package that CRAN
has since archived. A lookup against today's CRAN calls those unknown, and
they are nearly all of R's secondary column.

Off-registry software is not peculiar to Stata. In R it lives on GitHub.
`{python} f"{share_r_code_host:.1%}"` of R deposits load a package that CRAN
and Bioconductor lack and that the deposit itself installs with
`install_github` or a relative. A name is credited to a code host only when the same deposit installs it from one.
Pooling the evidence would let one deposit's `install_github("someone/utils")`
vouch for every unresolved `utils` in the corpus. Relaxing the rule to names
installed from a code host anywhere in the corpus would account for
`{python} f"{n_r_hosted_elsewhere_deposits:,}"` of the
`{python} f"{n_r_unknown_deposits:,}"` R deposits with an unresolved name.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-residue
table(
    residue_table,
    caption="Names no archive accounts for, labeled by hand",
    label="tab:residue",
    align="lrl",
    note=(
        f"Every name used in at least {RESIDUE_MIN_DEPOSITS} deposits that "
        "resolves to nothing, in all three languages, looked up one at a time. "
        "The labeled file is released with the data."
    ),
)
```

What is left is short enough to read. `{python} f"{n_residue_names:,}"`
names appear in at least `{python} f"{RESIDUE_MIN_DEPOSITS}"` deposits and
resolve to nothing. I looked each one up (\cref{tab:residue}).
`{python} f"{n_residue_software:,}"` are software. The other
`{python} f"{n_residue_not_software:,}"` are not: commands official Stata
ships without documenting, programs a deposit defines for itself, and text
the lexer read as code. Below that threshold sit
`{python} f"{n_unresolved_stata_singletons:,}"` Stata names that each appear
in one deposit: typos, macro fragments and one author's helpers.

Stata is hard to count because its software has no single registry. An index
removes that difficulty.

`{python} top_stata_package` is the most loaded Stata package in

Second place differs by field. Across the

## Discussion and Recommendations

### What better counts are for

These counts have two uses. The first is credit. A package in
`{python} f"{top_stata_share:.0%}"` of the Stata deposits at verified journals
gives its author a number that anyone can look up in the released tables.

The second is choosing what to test. Work on software reliability has to pick
packages to examine, and picking by reputation reproduces what the field
already believes. The companion project `kasauti` probes every release of a
package for results that changed without notice, and it picks its targets
partly by how often a function appears in real code. Validated-use counts
answer that question, and they point at the packages where a silent change
would touch the most published work.

### Limitations

Costly to inflate is not impossible to inflate. An author can load a package
they did not need, and a package bundled into a template that circulates in a
subfield collects counts without anyone choosing it. The unit cost is the
cost of a paper, not of a package, so the measure resists the cheap
manipulation that download counts invite and not a determined one.

The counts weight every deposit alike. A package used once in each of fifty
short papers and one used throughout a single large project score fifty to
one. That answers "how many pieces of research chose this" and not "how much
research depends on this".

The corpus comes from two collections with different instruments behind them.
The Harvard Dataverse material is a January 2024 scrape that kept only `.do`,
`.r` and `.py` files; the Zenodo material is whole deposits, including
notebooks, knitr documents and `.ado` files. A package used mainly inside a
literate document is under-counted on the Dataverse side, and the two
collections are two years apart. Recomputing every ranking on the file types
both collections share shows what that costs. For Stata and R all twenty top
places hold. For Python, `ipython` and `spacy` drop out of the top twenty and
four other packages move, none above rank fourteen; Python is the language
whose code most often lives in a notebook. The top ten in every language, the part the tables print, does not change.

Deposits whose archives exceed the size cap yield no code, and they are
code-heavy: the median archive in the smallest quartile holds
`{python} f"{code_files_smallest}"` code files and the median in the largest
holds `{python} f"{code_files_largest}"`. `{python} f"{n_spanned_deposits}"`
deposits split a package across `.z01`, `.7z.002` or `.partN.rar` segments,
which are not reassembled; only the last segment carries the archive's
directory, so the download completes and the first read fails.

Stata resolution reflects a command's status today, not its status when the
code was written. A command that was user-written in 2010 and later absorbed
into official Stata resolves as official, which can manufacture a trend for
anyone reading these counts over time.

Two false positives remain: SSC packages whose only command is a single
common token attract stray matches from Mata-style assignments outside a
`mata:` block. At present they are `{python} residual_false_positives`.

The lexer still reads some text as code. A do-file can hold prose an author
never commented out, log output pasted back into the script, and fragments of
Mata or R outside any block the lexer recognizes, and their first words land
in command position. `{python} f"{n_residue_not_software}"` of the
`{python} f"{n_residue_names}"` names in \cref{tab:residue} are of this kind,
`the` and `this` among them, and Stata keywords account for
`{python} f"{n_keyword_noise:,}"` more mentions across
`{python} f"{n_keyword_noise_deposits}"` deposits. They inflate the
unresolved rate and nothing else: a word of English cannot collide with a
package name.

The index of authors' sites is bounded by the corpus. SSC and the two
journals are crawled whole, but a site is found only if some deposit installs
from it or if looking up an unplaced name led to it. Software served from a
site no deposit names stays unresolved. Sites also die:
`{python} f"{n_net_unreachable}"` of the addresses deposits install from no
longer serve a manifest, and for some commands, `btscs` among them, the only
copies left are the ones authors shipped inside their deposits.

Julia files are collected and not parsed, so Julia is reported as language
presence only, as are MATLAB, SAS and SPSS. MATLAB has no import statement
and no registry to resolve against.

Which version ran is mostly not recorded. Code names the packages it loads
and almost never the release, so these counts pool a package across its
history. Where a file does say, the release records it: a Stata `version`
statement in `{python} f"{n_stata_version:,}"` of the
`{python} f"{n_stata_version_of:,}"` deposits holding a do-file, an
`renv.lock` or a bundled `DESCRIPTION` in `{python} f"{n_r_version}"` of
`{python} f"{n_r_version_of:,}"` deposits with R code, and a notebook's own
record of the interpreter that ran it. At
`{python} f"{share_stata_version:.0%}"` coverage for the best of these, the
environment table supports checking particular deposits and not estimating a
distribution.

### Recommendations

Research software is credited badly because the numbers available to credit
it with are cheap to produce. This paper offers one that is not: a count of
the packages that published, verified replication code loads, over
`{python} f"{n_deposits_analyzable:,}"` deposits and
`{python} f"{len(usage):,}"` packages.

The software social science leans on hardest, `{python} top_stata_package`
first, prepares exhibits, and a download count does not show that. The
language most of this code is written in was left out of studies of research
software for want of an index, and the index is now public. Registries miss
something in every language: in Stata, two journals' archives and authors'
sites; in R, GitHub.

A committee cannot reward what it cannot count [@sood_countpy]. Evaluation
committees and the designers of credit systems should use validated use where
they now use downloads or citations to software papers. Moving it by one
costs a published, verified paper, a build server cannot inflate it, and every
package's count is published.

## Data and code availability

The Stata command-to-package index is deposited at
[10.5281/zenodo.21926099](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21926099) under CC0,
with `{python} f"{n_index_commands:,}"` commands across
`{python} f"{n_index_packages:,}"` packages, as a record of its own.

The mention-level record and the aggregates are deposited at
[10.5281/zenodo.21943908](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21943908) under CC0,
covering `{python} f"{len(usage):,}"` packages, with counts by year and by
journal. Each mention carries its package, the function where the source
names one, the file, the line and a snippet, so the counts can be recomputed
without re-parsing the corpus. The deposited code itself,
`{python} f"{n_files:,}"` files, stays at the archives it came from. The
tables are also served at <https://recite.github.io/softverse/data/>, and each
package can be looked up at <https://recite.github.io/softverse/lookup/>. Both
DOIs resolve to the latest version of their record.

The extraction pipeline, the resolver and the sampling frame are at
<https://github.com/recite/softverse>.

## Reproducibility

The corpus, the registry snapshots, the download counts and the extractor are
pinned, and the first appendix lists each pin. Every mention carries the
extractor version and the registry lock that produced it.
