# Appendix: Validation of static parsing {#sec-baseline}

```{python}
#| label: resolution
res = candidates["resolution"].value_counts()
resolved = res.get("known_current", 0) + res.get("known_archived", 0)
unknown_share = res.get("unknown", 0) / len(candidates)
by_language = (
    candidates.assign(unresolved=candidates["resolution"].eq("unknown"))
    .groupby("language")["unresolved"]
    .agg(["size", "sum"])
)
by_language["rate"] = (by_language["sum"] / by_language["size"]).map("{:.1%}".format)
by_language.columns = ["candidate mentions", "unresolved", "rate"]
_res = by_language.sort_values("candidate mentions", ascending=False).reset_index()
_res.columns = ["language", "candidate mentions", "unresolved", "rate"]
table(
    _res,
    caption="Mentions that could name a package, and those left unresolved",
    label="tab:resolution",
    note=(
        "Restricted to mentions that could name a third-party package, so "
        "Stata builtins, standard libraries and programs a deposit defines "
        "itself are excluded from both columns. An unresolved mention is one "
        "the resolver cannot attribute, and not evidence that no package exists."
    ),
)
```

### Coverage

Resolution measures coverage, not precision: a deposit's own module can share
a name with a real distribution and still resolve.
`{python} f"{unknown_share:.1%}"` of the mentions that could name a
third-party package resolve to no registry, and the released tables list
every such name.

The denominator matters. Against all mentions the same rate is
`{python} f"{naive_unknown_share:.1%}"`, because that denominator includes
`{python} f"{n_stata_builtin_calls:,}"` calls to official Stata commands that
could never be unresolved. The rate above, over mentions that could name a
package, is `{python} f"{unknown_share / naive_unknown_share:.0f}"` times
larger.

Per deposit, the unresolved share is far below the pooled rate
(\cref{tab:unresolved}).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-unresolved
table(
    pd.DataFrame(
        [
            ("pooled over mentions", f"{unknown_share:.1%}"),
            ("median deposit", f"{median_deposit_unresolved:.1%}"),
            ("90th-percentile deposit", f"{p90_deposit_unresolved:.1%}"),
            ("deposits fully resolved", f"{share_deposits_fully_resolved:.0%}"),
        ],
        columns=["statistic", "unresolved share"],
    ),
    caption="Unresolved share, pooled and per deposit",
    label="tab:unresolved",
    note=(
        "Restricted to mentions that could name a third-party package. A "
        "minority of deposits hold most of the unresolved mentions."
    ),
)
```

Every candidate mention resolves in
`{python} f"{share_deposits_fully_resolved:.0%}"` of deposits.

Stata holds `{python} f"{stata_unknown_share_of_all:.0%}"` of all unresolved
mentions, spread over `{python} f"{n_unresolved_stata_names:,}"` names, of
which `{python} f"{n_unresolved_stata_singletons:,}"` appear in a single
deposit. The most widespread, `{python} top_unresolved_stata`, is in
`{python} f"{n_top_unresolved_deposits:,}"` deposits. \cref{tab:residue}
accounts for every name above the labeling threshold; below it are lexer
errors and authors' own programs.

Two kinds of name are neither resolved nor unresolved.
`{python} f"{n_local_relative:,}"` are Python imports of a module in the
deposit itself, relative (`from .models import Constants`) or absolute when a
file of that name sits in the deposit. `{python} f"{n_dynamic:,}"` are names
built at run time, as in `library(pkg, character.only = TRUE)`, where the
package is a variable. Both are reported in their own categories, since
`models`, `results` and `log` are PyPI distributions as well as names people
give their own files.

### Official Stata commands

An omission from the list of official Stata commands does damage: a command
Stata provides that the list lacks falls through to the SSC index, and if a
package ships a file of that name, the use is credited to the package. Every
command name in the corpus was therefore checked against StataCorp's public
help server. The server answers only for commands with a help page, and Stata
ships utilities without one, `_dots` and `tset` among them, so the list also
takes every `.ado` file name in the base directory of a Stata installation,
read from a public container build: `{python} f"{n_base_ado:,}"` names.

The check moved `{python} f"{n_verified_added}"` commands, including `ds`,
`pca` and `testparm`, from unresolved to official, and it removed every case
where a command claimed by both official Stata and an SSC package had been
credited to the package. With the curated list alone, the unresolved rate on
this corpus is `{python} f"{curated_only_share:.1%}"` against
`{python} f"{unknown_share:.1%}"`, and `{python} f"{n_misattributed:,}"`
mentions would have gone to an SSC package that ships a file of the same
name. The help server returns HTTP 200 for every query, so existence is read
from the page text, and pages from the User's Guide and the function manual
are excluded, since they document `_n`, `_b` and `e()`, which are not
commands.

### Agreement with `renv`

`renv::dependencies()` (`{python} renv_version`), run over
`{python} f"{n_renv_compared:,}"` of the corpus's
`{python} f"{n_r_deposits:,}"` R deposits, gives a mean per-deposit Jaccard
of `{python} f"{renv_mean_jaccard:.2f}"` and a pooled Jaccard of
`{python} f"{renv_pooled_jaccard:.2f}"`, and
`{python} f"{renv_perfect_share:.0%}"` of deposits agree exactly. The mean
weights every deposit equally and the pooled figure every package-deposit
pair. `{python} f"{n_renv_unreadable:,}"` deposits are excluded because renv
returned nothing for them: it runs with `errors = "ignored"` and skips a file
it cannot decode.

The comparison sets aside three kinds of name that renv reports and this extractor leaves out: `{python} f"{n_renv_aside_base:,}"` base R
packages such as `grid` and `stats`; `{python} f"{n_renv_aside_rmarkdown:,}"`
cases of `rmarkdown`, which renv adds for any `.Rmd` file; and
`{python} f"{n_renv_aside_outside:,}"` names found only in files outside the
analysis set, such as a package library shipped inside a deposit. Without
setting these aside, the mean Jaccard is
`{python} f"{renv_raw_mean_jaccard:.2f}"` and the pooled Jaccard
`{python} f"{renv_raw_pooled_jaccard:.2f}"`. After it, renv names
`{python} f"{n_renv_theirs_only:,}"` packages this extractor does not, and
this extractor names `{python} f"{n_renv_ours_only:,}"` that renv does not.

This is agreement between two static scans of the same files, and it is
weaker than accuracy: a package named only in a string, or loaded through a
variable, is invisible to both.

### Agreement with R's parser

Whether a file contains a call to `library` with argument `x` has an exact
answer, given by R's own parser. Running R's parser over
`{python} f"{n_oracle_files:,}"` `.R` files from both repositories and
walking its expression trees gives precision
`{python} f"{oracle_precision:.4f}"` and recall
`{python} f"{oracle_recall:.4f}"` over `{python} f"{n_oracle_pairs:,}"`
name-file pairs, `{python} f"{n_oracle_dataverse_files:,}"` of the files from
Dataverse. `{python} f"{n_oracle_unparseable:,}"` files that R could not parse
are excluded. The oracle's own walk had to handle a one-element result, a
`character.only = T` written with the symbol `T`, calls such as
`base::library(c)`, and `pkg::fun()` used as a default argument; the one
disagreement that was the extractor's error, `"m"::baz()` with a string on
the left, is fixed.

The extractor also runs, as a test, against `renv`'s own test fixture, which
lists thirteen ways of loading a package and states which must be found.

This check covers one thing exactly: whether the syntax walk sees what R
sees. It says nothing about Stata, about resolution against CRAN, or about
whether a `library()` call means the analysis used the package. No sample has
been labeled by hand for use, so there is no precision or recall against
research use.

### Code that nothing runs

A deposit can hold scripts nothing runs: an old draft, a helper that was
replaced, a figure cut in review. Where a deposit has a master script, the
files it reaches can be told from the files it does not, and the counts can be
recomputed over the reachable ones.

A master is a script that runs other scripts and is run by none, through
`source()`, `do`, `run`, `include` or a local import.
`{python} f"{n_graph_master:,}"` of `{python} f"{n_graph_considered:,}"`
deposits have one, and in `{python} f"{n_graph_complete:,}"` of those every
edge could be followed. The rest mostly build a path from a macro, as in
`do "$root/clean.do"`, which names a file only at run time;
`{python} f"{n_macro_edges:,}"` edges are written that way, against
`{python} f"{n_followed_edges:,}"` that could be followed. Counting a macro
edge as unreachable would report an idiom as dead code, so those deposits are
left out.

In the deposits with a complete graph,
`{python} f"{share_files_reachable:.0%}"` of analyzable files are reachable
from the master, and the median deposit has
`{python} f"{median_share_reachable:.0%}"` of its files on that path.
Recomputed over reachable files alone, the twenty most used packages keep a
median `{python} f"{reach_retained['stata']:.0%}"` of their Stata deposits,
`{python} f"{reach_retained['r']:.0%}"` of their R deposits and
`{python} f"{reach_retained['python']:.0%}"` of their Python deposits. The
package hit hardest keeps `{python} f"{min(reach_worst.values()):.0%}"`, and
no package moves more than `{python} f"{max_rank_move}"` places. The counts
shrink and the order holds.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-reachability
table(
    reach_table,
    caption="Counts over every analyzable file, and over files a master script reaches",
    label="tab:reachability",
    align="llrrll",
    note=(
        "The five most loaded packages per language. Restricted to deposits "
        "with a master script and a graph containing no edge that could not "
        "be followed. \\emph{Kept} is the share of the deposits that survive "
        "the restriction; \\emph{Rank} gives the package's position before "
        "and after it."
    ),
)
```

This check has two limits. It says nothing about the
`{python} f"{n_graph_considered - n_graph_master:,}"` deposits with no master
script, which are most of them. And a file a master reaches can still load a
package inside a branch that never runs, which no static reader can see.
